passage: Tuesday, 10 pm. Before I open a single book for the group report, I wrote what “done” means, on the first page of my notebook: (1) all four sections written, (2) numbers checked against the data sheet, (3) Raghav has read it once, (4) sent to the professor by Friday 5 pm. I've never done this before. Usually I work until it feels finished, and then it's never quite finished. I feel a bit silly staring at four lines, but they also feel like a fence around the work. Something has an end now. If Raghav's reading takes too long I'll still send by five. Friday 5:02 update: sent. It was good enough, and the evening is mine. — Sarika

qa.q: By what time on Friday did Sarika plan to send the report?
qa.a: Sarika planned to send the report to the professor by Friday at 5 pm.

qa.q: How does Sarika feel about the four lines on the first page?
qa.a: Sarika feels a bit silly at first but also comforted, because the four lines feel like a fence around the work.

qa.q: What difference did writing the endpoint make to Sarika's Friday?
qa.a: The clear list made stopping a decision rather than a drift, so Sarika sent the report at 5:02 and kept the evening free.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel about being one of the checkpoints?
qa.a: Raghav probably feels trusted and useful, and knows exactly what is expected: one reading, not an endless review.

grounding: A worker writes what finished looks like before starting, so there is no vague ninety percent.

passage:
Tejas: when do you stop working on something?
Charu: I write what done means first. for the sorting program it's: passes the three test files, comments written, emailed to ma'am
Tejas: that's it?
Charu: that's it. before, I'd keep tweaking forever 😅
Tejas: but what if it could be better
Charu: then it's version two. done is a promise to myself
Tejas: hmm. ok let me try for my lab record
Tejas: done = all 8 experiments copied, diagrams labelled, signed by Friday
Charu: love it. now stop at 5 on Friday 🙂
Tejas: even if I want to keep polishing?
Charu: especially then

qa.q: What does Charu's definition of done include for the sorting program?
qa.a: Charu's done means it passes the three test files, comments are written and it is emailed to ma'am.

qa.q: What does Tejas feel when asking whether it could be better?
qa.a: Tejas feels the pull of perfectionism and some doubt: “what if it could be better” shows a worry about stopping too early.

qa.q: What did Tejas write for the lab record, and what would it change?
qa.a: Tejas wrote: all eight experiments copied, diagrams labelled, signed by Friday, which gives a clear ending instead of an open-ended polish.

qa.q: How might Charu see the old habit of tweaking forever?
qa.a: Charu remembers it with a slightly embarrassed laugh and now treats “done” as a promise to Charu, so stopping is a choice.

grounding: A wise worker defines finished in advance, such as passing tests, commented and sent, so stopping is a decision.
